caption_hook: Washington was swept by giant floods, buried in lava and built from islands bolted onto the coast.

layers.name: MISSOULA FLOOD GRAVEL
layers.what: Ice dams in Montana burst again and again, sending walls of water across eastern Washington. The floods ripped out the Channeled Scablands and dumped giant gravel bars and boulders.
layers.bonus: Dry Falls, left by those floods, was once a waterfall about five times wider than Niagara.

layers.name: COLUMBIA RIVER BASALT
layers.hook: Lava floods that buried a region
layers.what: Runny lava poured from long cracks in the ground, flood after flood, until eastern Washington lay under thousands of feet of black basalt. Cooling split it into tall columns.
layers.bonus: Some of the flows ran all the way to the Pacific coast, about 300 miles away.

layers.name: CHUCKANUT FORMATION
layers.what: Rivers wound across a warm, swampy delta here, and their sand buried palm fronds, ferns and giant leaves. Now sandstone, it holds fossil leaf prints in cliffs near Bellingham.
layers.bonus: Scenic Chuckanut Drive winds along the cliffs of this very sandstone.

layers.name: CRESCENT FORMATION
layers.what: Undersea volcanoes and islands drifted in and were scraped onto the edge of North America. Their dark lavas now form the rugged mountains ringing the Olympic Peninsula.
layers.bonus: The rock is named after Lake Crescent in Olympic National Park.

layers.name: MOUNT STUART BATHOLITH
layers.hook: Magma that never reached the sky
layers.what: Deep underground, a huge body of molten rock cooled slowly into granite. Uplift and glaciers later exposed it as the jagged Stuart Range and the Enchantments.
layers.bonus: Mount Stuart, 9,415 ft, is the second-highest non-volcanic peak in Washington.

layers.name: BELT SUPERGROUP
layers.hook: Mud from a lost inland sea
layers.what: Long before animals, rivers fed mud and sand into a vast basin in what is now the Northern Rockies. Squeezed into hard slate and quartzite, those layers reach northeast Washington.
layers.bonus: The same family of rock forms the soaring cliffs of Glacier National Park in Montana.
